clue.text: Permit those finally excluded before sixteen, for example, to vote

indicators.note: placed before tells us which piece comes first when the parts are joined
what is excluded is left out, so a letter is struck from the word before it

parts.note: to suffer something is to allow it, as in 'suffer the little children'

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is wanted

parts.note: the closing letter of 'those'
sixteen is an example of an age

explanation.surface: A campaigner argues that sixteen-year-olds, once left out, should now be allowed to vote.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface about votes at sixteen makes 'vote' look like part of the campaign, but it is the definition. 'Permit' is the old sense of suffer, as in 'suffer the little children'.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffrage is the right to cast a ballot in elections, a formal synonym for the franchise or vote.

clue.text: The Spanish attack Sweden, lifting blockade

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting means reading from the bottom upward, so the order is turned around

parts.note: el is Spanish for 'the'
a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: Spanish forces strike at Sweden and so break a blockade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting blockade' reads like the end of a siege, but 'lifting' is the turning signal and 'blockade' is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stifle something is to smother or choke it off, much as a blockade cuts off supplies and movement.

clue.text: Can't travel so amazingly far at this length

indicators.note: something done amazingly is done in a startling, unexpected way, so the letters land in a surprising new order

parts.note: the letters of the last four words, used as written

explanation.surface: Someone marvels that it is impossible to journey so far over such a distance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: by the laws of physics nothing can travel at that speed, so 'Can't travel so' points at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Relativity forbids any object from exceeding the speed of light, so that is precisely the manner in which travel is impossible.

clue.text: Get to stretch

definitions.meaning: first meaning: arrive at a place
second meaning: extend an arm out, or a stretch of river

explanation.walkthrough: The three words read as one instruction, but they split into two separate meanings of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means arrive at a destination; as a noun or verb it means the extent one can extend an arm.

clue.text: Won work with last two pieces of apricot crumble

parts.note: to have won something is to have got it
OP is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the final pair of pieces means only the closing couple of letters are kept

parts.note: the closing pair of letters of 'apricot'

explanation.surface: A baker wins with a fruit crumble, its last two pieces of apricot on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apricot crumble' looks like a dessert, but 'crumble' is the definition, used as a verb meaning decay. The wordplay chunks cut across the three words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pot is an idiom for falling into ruin or decay, which is what something does when it crumbles.

clue.text: Plaster minor injuries around clot unevenly

indicators.note: to come around is to turn back on oneself, so the word runs the other way

parts.note: cuts are small wounds

indicators.note: uneven means odd-numbered, so only the first, third and so on letters are taken

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of 'clot'

explanation.surface: Someone puts a plaster on small wounds around a blood clot that has formed unevenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plaster' looks like a sticking plaster for the injuries, but it is the building material for walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine lime or cement render applied to walls, a kind of decorative exterior plaster.

clue.text: One plays spin or net shot

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up and reformed

parts.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A player chooses between a spinning shot and one at the net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like a tennis stroke, completing the picture, but it is the anagram signal. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional coach at a club is someone who plays the game for a living, so 'one plays' is a loose description.

clue.text: Pudding cooked in the Colosseum with coal after lira abolished

indicators.note: cooking transforms raw ingredients, so the letters are mixed into a new form
what is abolished is done away with, so that letter is struck out

parts.note: the letters as written
the letters as written
L is the abbreviation for the lira, the old Italian currency

explanation.surface: A dessert is baked in the Roman amphitheatre over coal, after Italy gave up its old currency.
explanation.walkthrough: L leaves COAL, and the remaining COA joins the letters of THE COLOSSEUM to be rearranged. The Italian setting suits the lira, which gave way to the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain 'pudding' is the general word for dessert, and a chocolate mousse is a light whipped dessert.

clue.text: How 11 is written gradually

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the numeral consists of a 1 placed beside another 1
second meaning: a single item at a time, in steady succession

explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like a cross-reference to another clue, but it is simply the number eleven, whose two digits stand side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing things singly, each after the last, is proceeding slowly in stages, which is the sense of gradually.

clue.text: Ticks example broadcast

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard by listeners, so we want a word that sounds right rather than one spelt right

parts.note: an instance is an example

explanation.surface: A televised illustration of how ticks behave, as in a nature programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ticks' suggests insects or check marks, but here it means moments, as in 'back in a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tick is British informal speech for a very brief moment, and so is an instant.

clue.text: Cheers, episode nine: Crane openly ridicules European capitals

definitions.note: plural noun for a singular answer; the shout is itself a cheer

indicators.note: capitals are the large letters that begin words, so each word supplies only its opening letter

parts.words: episode nine: Crane openly ridicules European
parts.note: the opening letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A TV guide note: in an episode of the sitcom Cheers, Frasier Crane mocks European capital cities.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers was an American sitcom featuring psychiatrist Frasier Crane, so 'Cheers' looks like the show's title and 'capitals' like cities.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience calling for more at the end of a show shouts it as applause, a form of cheering.

clue.text: 3 down by hard box or plane, perhaps

indicators.note: being down by something means being short of it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the number written out as a word
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to another clue, then a box or an aircraft, which reads like nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: '3 down' looks like a pointer to the clue for REACH, but 3 is just the number and 'down by' means short of. THREE minus H leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Box and plane are both species of woody plant, so each is an example of the general category; 'perhaps' flags the examples.

clue.text: Sucker punch, no joke, gets past protection

indicators.note: getting past something means coming after it, so this piece is placed second

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind

indicators.note: 'no' says that something is absent, so those letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: the word as written
a pun is a play on words, a joke

explanation.surface: A boxer lands a surprise blow, no laughing matter, that slips through the opponent's guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker punch' reads as one phrase, but 'Sucker' is the definition and 'punch' begins the wordplay. The lee is the side sheltered from the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A leech is a blood-sucking worm, and figuratively a parasite who sucks resources from others.

clue.text: Economy Ministry traffic follows what is expected

indicators.note: to follow is to come after, so the earlier-named item is placed second

parts.note: par is the expected standard, as in golf
simony is the buying and selling of church offices, trade in ministry

explanation.surface: A government department's road congestion is exactly as predicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Economy Ministry' reads like a finance department and 'traffic' like cars, but traffic here means illicit trade, and ministry means church office.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsimony is extreme frugality or thrift, a stingier version of careful saving with money.

clue.text: Sound quality pioneered by soprano

indicators.note: what is pioneered by someone is led by them, so that piece goes at the front

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for soprano
a trait is a characteristic quality

explanation.surface: A particular tone colour of singing first developed by a soprano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound quality' looks like audio timbre in a musical scene, but 'Sound' is a narrow stretch of sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound is a narrow channel of water between two landmasses, which is also what a strait is.

clue.text: Instrument built from gold I removed from laboratories

indicators.note: building from raw materials puts them together in a new arrangement
taking something away from a word leaves it short of those letters

parts.note: the letters as written
or is gold in heraldry
taken as written

explanation.surface: A device made in a lab from gold, with one scientist stepping away.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing OR and I from LABORATORIES leaves nine letters, which are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrolabe is an ancient astronomical device for measuring the altitude of stars, so it is a scientific instrument.

clue.text: It marks the spot General is picked up and run over

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the words are judged by how they are said

parts.note: X marks the spot on a map, and plain means general or ordinary

explanation.surface: On a treasure map, a cross shows where a general was lifted up and driven over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like an army officer, but here it is the adjective meaning common or everyday. Said aloud, the letter and that word make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To run over something is to go through it again in detail so it is understood, which is clarifying.

clue.text: Washington rose up after enslavement as tool

indicators.note: coming after puts this piece second in the line

parts.note: to be in chains is to be enslaved

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom up, so the letters run backward

parts.note: WA is the postal abbreviation for Washington state

explanation.surface: A history note: Washington rebelled after being held in bondage, as a mere instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington' suggests George Washington and an uprising, but it is just the state abbreviation turned upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A chainsaw is a motor-driven cutting device with a toothed chain, a powered tool for felling.

clue.text: Try Tetris, mostly replaced by debut of Nintendo console

indicators.note: most of the word is swapped out for something else, leaving only its first part

parts.note: a judge will try or hear a case
the name of the puzzle game, as written, before most of it is swapped out

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of 'Nintendo'

explanation.surface: Play Tetris, now mostly superseded by Nintendo's first games machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Console' looks like a games console, but it is the verb meaning comfort. TRIS, the bigger part of TETRIS, gives way to N.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten someone is to cheer and encourage them, which is what one does when comforting a person in distress.

clue.text: Crazy for students to adopt ChatGPT's conclusion

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: NUS is the National Union of Students, the UK student body

indicators.note: a conclusion is the end, so the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of ChatGPT

explanation.surface: It is mad for students to embrace whatever the AI chatbot concludes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a jibe at students using AI, but ChatGPT only supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is informal for mad or insane, so it is a slang synonym for crazy.

clue.text: Court library is vacant

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them
a den is a study or private room for reading

explanation.surface: The courthouse library has nobody in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court library' reads as a law library, but Court is a verb and library a quiet room at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden expression shows no emotion, stiff and blank, much like a vacant stare.

clue.text: Charming ladies wear fashionable silk top (not new)

indicators.note: what one wears goes around the body, so one piece encloses another
'not new' asks for the abbreviation for new to be dropped

parts.note: ladies are women
in means fashionable

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of 'silk'

explanation.surface: Elegant women wear a stylish silk top that isn't brand new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wear' reads as dressing in the silk top, but it signals the shortened ladies wrapping round the fashionable piece and the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsome describes someone attractive in a sweet, engaging way, so it is a synonym for charming.

clue.text: Heads of major economies invested in small dollar denomination bond

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a cent is the smallest US coin, a hundredth of a dollar

indicators.note: heads are the first letters of the words that follow

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Leaders of the big economies put money into a low-value dollar bond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' looks like a financial security in this economics surface, but it is the verb meaning stick together.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement is to join firmly, as with mortar, and figuratively to strengthen a relationship.

clue.text: Some gains are realised from contents of stolen gilts

definitions.note: a sentence fragment completed by the adjective

indicators.note: realising means converting assets into new form, so the letters are turned into a different order
the contents are what lies inside, so the outer letters are discarded

parts.note: both words run together without their first and last letters

explanation.surface: Profits are cashed in from what was inside a haul of stolen government bonds.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilts are British government bonds. The definition finishes the phrase 'ill-gotten gains', and the whole surface backs it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Gains acquired dishonestly or illegally are described with this stock adjective, so the phrase completes the familiar idiom.

clue.text: What cow does with English deer

parts.note: a cow moos
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A question about how a cow behaves alongside an English deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is the joining word that adds the second piece to the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The moose is the largest species of the deer family, called an elk in Europe.

clue.text: Animal tallow extract in Mediterranean island

indicators.note: an extract is a portion drawn out of something bigger, so the letters are taken from within

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Rendered animal fat produced on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract' sounds like a product made from tallow, but it signals letters drawn from inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Malta is an island nation in the central Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily.

clue.text: Striking gesture

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a sign or motion made to communicate

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a blow or punch, but they are two separate meanings, one an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means remarkable or outstanding; as a noun it means a sign made with the hands.

clue.text: Blend fuel Tesco giving away to add energy

indicators.note: giving something away means no longer having it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: coal is a fuel
Tesco is the largest British supermarket chain
taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A supermarket chain hands out a fuel blend with added energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesco is Britain's biggest supermarket, which sells fuel at its stations. Taking TO out of it leaves ESC.
explanation.definitionFit: To coalesce is to come together and merge into a single whole, which is to combine or mix.

clue.text: Shrink accompanying medical facility

parts.note: with means accompanying
ER is the emergency room of a hospital

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist goes along with a patient to a clinic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like slang for a psychiatrist, but it is a verb meaning contract.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants wither when they dry up and shrivel, becoming smaller and weaker.

clue.text: Immoral and lacking heart — moral on the outside

indicators.note: sitting on the outside means wrapping around, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: decent means morally upright

indicators.note: without its heart a word keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of 'and'

explanation.surface: Someone is wicked and heartless, though respectable in outward appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a link word joining two descriptions, but it is fodder that loses its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes self-indulgent moral decline and luxury, so it serves as a synonym for immoral.
